{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"0cc151419b9a9e10f2600f2a263f07f595aef456dbf2596d2630dbdb5fc87f7d","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:103","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Belt and child restraint confusables and continuation details","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: back-seat belt ages, car seat versus booster bands, driver versus parent responsibility, belt fit for adults versus children, quoted crash statistics, hot-car heat levels and child abuse penalties","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: back-seat belt ages, car seat versus booster bands, driver versus parent responsibility, belt fit for adults versus children, quoted crash statistics, hot-car heat levels and child abuse penalties
Confusable pairs and continuation facts for the safety belt chapter; each block ties to one manual page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec06-R01 | anchor: A01
Back-seat belt rules depend on who is driving: passengers under 17 must belt in any case, and with a permit or intermediate driver the rule covers back-seat passengers aged four to 17. [A01]
Why it matters: group belt ages; confusable passenger age rule versus new-driver rule.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-R02 | anchor: A01
Car seat direction turns on age and weight: rear-facing below one year or 20 pounds, forward-facing from one through three above 20 pounds, then a booster from four through eight while under four feet, nine inches. [A01]
Why it matters: group child seats; confusable rear-facing, forward-facing and booster bands.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-R03 | anchor: A01
The plain $50 fine applies to a driver who fails to restrain a child under 16, while missing a required car seat or booster seat carries the heavier Class C misdemeanor penalty. [A01]
Why it matters: group penalties; confusable general restraint fine versus car seat offense.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-R04 | anchor: A01
Being ejected from a vehicle sharply raises the chance of death or serious injury, and the manual puts the chance of being killed by ejection at one in eight. [A01]
Why it matters: group belt benefits; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-R05 | anchor: A02
Belted occupants who do strike the wheel, dashboard or windshield usually hit with far less force and suffer less serious injury [A02] [A01].
Why it matters: group belt benefits; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R06 | anchor: A02
For light truck occupants, the manual says correct belt use lowers the risk of death by 60 percent and of moderate-to-critical injury by 65 percent. [A02]
Why it matters: group statistics; confusable car figures versus light truck figures.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R07 | anchor: A02
The manual reports that unbelted occupants were 32 times more likely to die and 3 times more likely to be seriously injured in a crash. [A02]
Why it matters: group statistics; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R08 | anchor: A02
According to the manual, only one-half of one percent of crashes end in fire or submersion, and staying conscious because of the belt improves your chance of escaping. [A02]
Why it matters: group myths; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R09 | anchor: A02
The manual says crashes on Tennessee roads killed 1039 people in 2016, many of whom might have lived had they buckled up. [A02]
Why it matters: group statistics; dated figure.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R10 | anchor: A02
The manual says infants properly secured in safety seats survive almost 75 percent of crashes that would otherwise kill them, and toddlers survive more than half. [A02]
Why it matters: group child seat benefits; confusable infant versus toddler survival.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R11 | anchor: A02
The manual states that correct use of child restraints could prevent 9 of 10 deaths and 8 of 10 serious injuries among child passengers under four. [A02]
Why it matters: group child seat benefits; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R12 | anchor: A02
Children copy their parents in the car, so buckling up yourself every trip sets the habit for your child. [A02]
Why it matters: group example; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R13 | anchor: A02
The CDC figures in the manual name motor vehicle crashes as the leading cause of fatal injury for children aged 3 to 14 in 2020. [A02]
Why it matters: group statistics; dated figure.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-R14 | anchor: A03
Once a child transitions out of a safety seat to vehicle belts, position the lap belt firmly across the upper thighs so it stays low and snug over the hips [A03].
Why it matters: group belt fit; confusable adult versus child lap belt.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-R15 | anchor: A03
The manual credits air bags with saving more than 39,976 lives between 1987 and 2012, citing NHTSA estimates. [A03]
Why it matters: group air bags; dated figure.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-R16 | anchor: A03
Infants in rear-facing seats belong in the rear seat of a vehicle that has a passenger air bag, if a rear seat is available. [A03]
Why it matters: group air bags; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-R17 | anchor: A03
Cities and counties may pass ordinances barring children aged 6 to 12 from pickup beds on local roads too. [A03]
Why it matters: group pickup beds; confusable state highway rule versus local ordinance.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-R18 | anchor: A04
On a mild 73-degree day an SUV can heat to 100 degrees in 10 minutes and 120 degrees in 30 minutes, and at 90 degrees outside the interior can reach 160 degrees within several minutes. [A04]
Why it matters: group hot cars; confusable mild-day versus hot-day figures.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec06-R19 | anchor: A04
Heat exhaustion can set in above 90 degrees and heat stroke above 105 degrees, and children's still-developing breathing systems make them especially vulnerable. [A04]
Why it matters: group hot cars; confusable heat exhaustion versus heat stroke thresholds.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec06-R20 | anchor: A04
Children can put a vehicle in motion, so always lock the car and keep keys and remote entry devices away from them. [A04]
Why it matters: group hot cars; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec06-R21 | anchor: A04
Under Tennessee child abuse law, knowingly injuring a child under 18 is a Class A misdemeanor, but it becomes a Class D felony when the child is six or younger. [A04]
Why it matters: group penalties; confusable child under eighteen versus six or younger.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec06-R22 | anchor: A04
A Class A misdemeanor can bring up to 11 months, 29 days in jail, a fine up to $2,500, or both, while a Class A felony carries 15 to 60 years and a possible fine up to $50,000. [A04]
Why it matters: group penalties; confusable misdemeanor versus felony ranges.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]
